paragraphs.modern: But as I was saying at the start, the truth, I think, is this: whether such practices are honorable or dishonorable is not a simple question. They are honorable to whoever pursues them honorably, and dishonorable to whoever pursues them dishonorably. There is dishonor in yielding to the bad, or yielding in a bad way; but there is honor in yielding to the good, or yielding in an honorable way. And the bad lover is the common lover, inspired by the Common Love, who loves the body rather than the soul; for he is not even stable, since he loves something that is itself unstable. So when the bloom of youth he desired is over, he takes wing and flies away, despite all his words and promises. But the man who loves a noble character stays for life, because his love becomes one with what is everlasting. The custom of our country wants both kinds of lover to be tested well and truly, and wants us to yield to the one sort and avoid the other. That is why it encourages lovers to pursue and the beloved to flee: it tests both lover and beloved in contests and trials, until each of them shows which of the two kinds he belongs to.
paragraphs.notes: Light fix on the accepted wording. Jowett's 'vulgar lover' becomes 'the common lover, inspired by the Common Love', tying it to 3.0-3.1 and 3.9; 4.3 treats 'the vulgar Polyhymnia' the same way. 'The love of the noble disposition' is read as the man who loves a noble character, set against the man who loves the body, as the assessor asked. Jowett's 'would have both of them proven' refers to the two sorts of lover, because his next clause is 'yield to the one sort of lover and avoid the other'. The accepted text had 'both lover and beloved' here, which repeated the later clause, so it now says 'both kinds of lover'. 'Some to pursue, and others to fly' is spelled out as lovers pursuing and the beloved fleeing.

paragraphs.modern: Pausanias came to a pause — there's a neat little jingle for you, in the balanced style the wise teachers of speaking have taught me. Aristodemus said that Aristophanes was due to speak next, but either because he had eaten too much or for some other reason, he had the hiccups and had to switch turns with Eryximachus the physician, who was reclining on the couch below him. 'Eryximachus,' said Aristophanes, 'you ought either to stop my hiccups or to speak in my place until they're over.'
paragraphs.notes: Aristophanes is now named and his line quoted. The aside is marked as a joke with 'a neat little jingle for you', and Jowett's ironic 'the wise' becomes 'the wise teachers of speaking'. 'Speak in my place' matches Eryximachus's reply in the kept 3.11 ('I'll speak in your place'). The kept 3.11 still has no quotation marks, which the assessor also noted, so a reviewer may want to add them to match.

paragraphs.modern: Eryximachus spoke as follows: 'Since Pausanias made a fine beginning but a lame ending, I must try to supply what he left out. I think he was right to distinguish two kinds of love. But my own art, medicine, informs me further that this double love is not merely a feeling in human souls, directed toward beautiful people or toward anything else. It is also found in the bodies of all animals, in all that grows from the earth, and, I may say, in everything that exists. That is the conclusion I seem to have drawn from my own art of medicine, which teaches me how great and wonderful and universal a god Love is: his empire extends over all things, divine as well as human. And I will begin with medicine, to honor my own art. The human body contains these two kinds of love. Everyone agrees that they are different and unlike, and because they are unlike, what they love and desire is unlike too: what is healthy desires one thing, and what is diseased desires another. Pausanias said a moment ago that it is honorable to gratify good men — to yield to their love — and dishonorable to gratify bad ones. In the same way, in the body the good and healthy elements should be gratified, while the bad elements, the elements of disease, should not be gratified but discouraged.
paragraphs.notes: Opens Eryximachus's speech with a single quote and leaves it open. There is no mark at the end of 4.0-4.4, and the quote closes at the end of 4.5, following the house pattern for multi-paragraph speeches (6.9 to 6.10). 'Indulge' becomes 'gratify', glossed with 'to yield to their love' to tie it to Pausanias's term in chapter 3. The same verb is used in 4.3 for Jowett's 'accepting'. Jowett attaches 'confessedly different and unlike' to the two kinds of love, and that attachment is kept. 'The fair' becomes 'beautiful people', and 'productions of the earth' becomes 'all that grows from the earth'.

paragraphs.modern: This is what the physician has to do, and this is what the art of medicine consists of. For medicine can be regarded, broadly speaking, as the knowledge of the body's loves and desires, and of how to satisfy them or not. The best physician is the one who can separate the good love from the bad, or turn one into the other. And a physician who knows how to root out love and how to plant it, whichever is needed, and who can reconcile the most hostile elements in the body's constitution and make them loving friends, is a skillful practitioner. Now the most hostile elements are the most opposite ones, such as hot and cold, bitter and sweet, moist and dry, and the like. My ancestor Asclepius — we doctors trace our descent from him — knew how to plant friendship and agreement in these elements, and so he created our art. That is what our poet friends here tell us, and I believe them. And not only medicine in all its branches, but also the arts of physical training and farming, are under his dominion. Anyone who gives the subject the slightest attention will also see that music involves the same reconciling of opposites. I suppose that must have been what Heracleitus meant, although he did not put it accurately. For he says that the One is united by disunion, like the harmony of the bow and the lyre, in which string and frame pull against each other and so hold together. Now it is absurd to say that harmony is discord, or that it is made up of elements that are still in a state of discord.
paragraphs.notes: 'Under his dominion' is kept with Jowett's pronoun and his word 'dominion', which echoes 'empire' in 4.0 as it does in Jowett. Grammatically, Jowett's sentence points to Asclepius. The assessor's reading, the god Love, depends on the wider speech and the Greek, so it is not imposed. If a reviewer prefers the Love reading, change 'under his dominion' to 'under Love's dominion'. Jowett's spelling 'Heracleitus' is restored under 'keep proper names as Jowett has them'; the accepted text had 'Heraclitus'. Added glosses: doctors trace their descent from Asclepius; 'our poet friends here' are the poets at the party; bow and lyre hold together because string and frame pull against each other. 'Gymnastic' becomes 'physical training', because the modern sport would mislead, and 'husbandry' becomes 'farming'. 'Fair love from foul' becomes 'the good love from the bad'.

paragraphs.modern: But what he probably meant was this: harmony is made of differing notes, of higher and lower pitch, that once disagreed but have now been reconciled by the art of music. For if the higher and lower notes still disagreed, there could be no harmony — clearly not. After all, harmony is consonance, that is, notes sounding together; and consonance is a kind of agreement. But there can be no agreement between things that disagree, as long as they still disagree: you cannot harmonize what disagrees. In the same way, rhythm is made up of short and long beats, which once differed but are now in accord. And just as medicine plants this agreement in the body, so music plants it in all these cases, making love and unison grow up among them. So music, too, is concerned with the principles of love, as they apply to harmony and rhythm. Again, if you look at harmony and rhythm in their essential nature, it is easy to make out love in them, and there love has not yet become double: it has not yet split into a good kind and a bad kind. But when you want to use them in actual life, either in composing songs or in correctly performing melodies and verses already composed — which is what we call education, since that is how the young are trained — then the difficulty begins, and a good artist is needed.
paragraphs.notes: 'Symphony' becomes 'consonance, that is, notes sounding together'. Jowett's 'which accordance' clause is recast as an explicit parallel: medicine plants agreement in the body, and music plants it in notes and beats. 'Love which has not yet become double' is glossed as 'not yet split into a good kind and a bad kind', which makes the theory-versus-practice contrast explicit. 'Airs or metres' becomes 'melodies and verses', which avoids 'meters' being heard as a unit of length. 'Which latter is called education' gets a short gloss: 'since that is how the young are trained'.

paragraphs.modern: At that point we must retell the old story of the beautiful and heavenly love, which in music is the love that comes from Urania, the beautiful and heavenly Muse. It tells of our duty to gratify the temperate, and to gratify those who are not yet temperate only so that they may become temperate, and to preserve their love. And again it tells of Polyhymnia, the common Muse of many songs, who stands in music for the Common Love. She must be used with caution, so that her pleasure is enjoyed without breeding licentiousness — just as in my own art it is no small task to regulate a gourmet's appetites, so that he can satisfy his tastes without the disease that comes with them. From this I conclude that in music, in medicine, and in all other things, human as well as divine, we must keep watch on both loves as far as we can, for both are present.
paragraphs.notes: The two Muses are tied to Pausanias's two loves: in music, the heavenly love is the love that comes from Urania, and Polyhymnia stands for the Common Love. 'Vulgar' becomes 'common', as in 3.6, and 'Muse of many songs' explains Polyhymnia's name. Jowett repeats 'fair and heavenly' for both the love and the Muse, and 'the beautiful and heavenly' keeps that echo. 'The Common Love' is capitalized as in 3.0, 3.6 and 3.9. 'Accepting' becomes 'gratify', as in 4.0, and the purpose clause is kept: the not-yet-temperate are gratified only so that they may become temperate. In Jowett, 'who must be used with circumspection' refers to Polyhymnia herself, so it stays 'she must be used with caution', which also sounds like a physician. 'A great matter' becomes 'no small task'. 'Epicure' becomes 'gourmet'.

paragraphs.modern: The course of the seasons, too, is full of both these principles. When, as I was saying, the elements of hot and cold, moist and dry, come to feel a harmonious love for one another and blend with moderation and harmony, they bring health and plenty to men, animals, and plants, and do them no harm. But when the unruly love gets the upper hand and takes hold of the seasons of the year, it does great damage and harm. It is the source of plagues, and it brings many other kinds of disease on animals and plants; for frost, hail, and blight all spring from the excesses and disorders of these elements of love. The study of these elements, as they relate to the movements of the heavenly bodies and to the seasons of the year, is called astronomy. Furthermore, all sacrifices, and the whole field of divination — the reading of signs from the gods, the art through which gods and men communicate — are concerned, I say, only with preserving the good love and curing the bad. For every kind of impiety is likely to follow if, instead of accepting, honoring, and revering the harmonious love in everything he does, a man honors the other love, whether in his feelings toward gods or parents, toward the living or the dead. That is why the task of divination is to watch over these loves and heal them; and divination is the peacemaker between gods and men, working through its knowledge of the pious and impious tendencies in human loves. Such is the great and mighty — or rather, the all-powerful — force of love in general.
paragraphs.notes: 'Wanton' becomes 'unruly' and 'pestilence' becomes 'plagues'. Jowett's fronted relative ('which to know in relation to') becomes its own sentence, and it defines astronomy's scope as the heavenly bodies and the seasons. Divination is glossed as 'the reading of signs from the gods'. 'Hoar-frost' becomes 'frost'. Jowett's 'accepting' is kept here (accepting the harmonious love), because in this sentence it reads naturally in present-day English. 'Religious or irreligious tendencies' becomes 'pious and impious tendencies', which matches 'impiety' earlier in the paragraph.

paragraphs.modern: And above all, it is the love concerned with the good that has the greatest power — the love that is perfected in company with temperance and justice, whether among gods or men. This love is the source of all our happiness and harmony, and it makes us friends with the gods above us and with one another. I suppose that I too have left out several things that might be said in praise of Love, but this was not intentional. And now, Aristophanes, you may make up for what I have omitted, or praise him in some other way; for I see that you are rid of your hiccups.'
paragraphs.notes: Closes Eryximachus's speech, which opens in 4.0. The main verb ('has the greatest power') now comes before the second relative clause. 'Hiccough' becomes 'hiccups', as in chapter 3.

paragraphs.modern: 'Yes,' said Aristophanes, who was next to speak, 'the hiccups are gone — though not until I applied the sneeze. And I wonder whether the harmony of the body has a love for such noises and ticklings, since no sooner had I applied the sneeze than I was cured.'
paragraphs.notes: Spelling and idiom only. 'Who followed' becomes 'who was next to speak'. 'Applied the sneeze' keeps the mock-medical verb, and 'the harmony of the body has a love for' keeps the parody of Eryximachus.

paragraphs.modern: Eryximachus said: 'Take care, my friend Aristophanes. You are about to speak, and yet you are making fun of me. So I shall have to keep an eye on your speech and see whether I can have a laugh at your expense, when you could otherwise speak in peace.'
paragraphs.notes: Jowett's 'although' becomes 'and yet', and his 'and' becomes 'so', which makes the threat explicit: because Aristophanes is joking before his own speech, Eryximachus will watch that speech for something to laugh at. 'Whether I cannot have a laugh' loses its double negative.

paragraphs.modern: 'You are right,' said Aristophanes, laughing. 'I take back what I said. But please don't watch me, because I'm afraid that in the speech I am about to make, instead of people laughing with me — which comes naturally to our comic muse and would be all to the good — they will only laugh at me.'
paragraphs.notes: 'I will unsay my words' becomes 'I take back what I said'. 'Which is to the manner born of our muse' becomes 'which comes naturally to our comic muse', and 'our muse' is made explicit as comedy. The distinction between laughing with him and laughing at him is kept.
